name: UNM

profile.address: 2701, Campus Boulevard Northeast, Nob Hill, Albuquerque, Bernalillo County, New Mexico, 87106
profile.reading:
This building is a data center on the University of New Mexico's Albuquerque campus, at an address on Campus Boulevard Northeast in the Nob Hill area near the university's core. It serves UNM, a public research university and the state's flagship institution, though the specific campus department responsible for this particular building was not confirmed through public materials, and UNM does not appear to publish a dedicated public facing page describing this building by name.

UNM operates more than one facility that could plausibly be described publicly as a data center. The university's central information technology division, UNM Information Technologies, is responsible for the administrative, academic, and network systems that keep the broader university running, from student records and financial systems to email and campus networking, and a central IT organization of that scope typically requires a dedicated enterprise data center of some kind. Separately, UNM's Center for Advanced Research Computing, known as CARC, operates high performance computing clusters, including systems named Hopper and Easley, for faculty and student researchers across the university, out of a facility at a different Albuquerque address on Central Avenue Northeast, several blocks from the Campus Boulevard site associated with this building. Because the Campus Boulevard address does not match CARC's published location, this building most likely houses a separate, general purpose enterprise data center operated by UNM's central IT organization rather than CARC's research computing facility, though that has not been independently confirmed through a UNM statement naming the building.

As is typical for a public university's internal data center, UNM does not publish building level statistics such as square footage, power capacity, redundancy design, or construction history for this facility, and no news coverage, permit filing, or property record describing it by name was located. This is not unusual. University enterprise data centers exist to keep internal systems running rather than to attract outside tenants or public attention, and institutions generally see little reason to publicize engineering details about buildings that host no public facing service beyond the university's own IT operations. What can be said with confidence is that the building sits within UNM's central campus footprint, consistent with a facility built to serve the university's own administrative and network infrastructure needs close to the offices and systems it supports.

reading:
The University of New Mexico is the state's flagship public research university, in Albuquerque, and like most large universities it runs computing plant for itself rather than for tenants. It appears in this registry with a single row, and the useful work here is establishing which of UNM's two quite separate computing organisations that row actually points at.

The row is a point, not a building outline. It was created in OpenStreetMap on 1 December 2024, tagged as a data centre with UNM as operator and the address 2701 Campus Boulevard NE, Albuquerque 87106. Checked against UNM's own campus map, the point falls about 38 metres from the Information Technologies Building, also carried on the map as the R-IT Building, with the R Lot Information Technologies car park immediately alongside and the Campus Utility Plant about 85 metres to the west. So the row is UNM Information Technologies on Campus Boulevard NE, north of the main campus. It carries no floor area, no construction date, no power figure and no building geometry, because it is an addressed point and nothing more.

That is not the university's research computing facility. UNM's Center for Advanced Research Computing is a separate operation at 1601 Central Avenue NE, on the Route 66 corridor rather than Campus Boulevard, founded in 1994 and funded through the Office of the Vice President for Research. CARC publishes machine specifications rather than facility specifications, and they are current and detailed. Easley, a mixed processor and accelerator cluster, has 65 compute nodes, 4,160 CPU cores, 23.3 terabytes of memory, 36 NVIDIA L40S and 8 H100 accelerators, on an NVIDIA NDR 800 gigabit InfiniBand fabric. Hopper has 61 nodes, 2,176 cores and 37 A100 accelerators on HDR 400 gigabit InfiniBand. Xena, the oldest of the three, has 32 nodes, 720 cores and K40 accelerators on 56 gigabit FDR. Across the centre, UNM advertises more than 6,300 cores, more than 80 accelerators, more than five petabytes of storage and 100 gigabit networking, provided without charge to UNM faculty, staff and students. Tyson Swetnam was named director in the most recent leadership change, succeeding Patrick Bridges.

What neither organisation publishes is anything about the rooms. CARC's own description of its machine rooms is generic, noting only raised floors and hot aisle containment to keep supply and return air separated. Neither UNM Information Technologies nor CARC discloses a white space area, an IT load, a utility service size, a generator count or a cooling design for either building, and no county permit or state filing establishing those figures was located. That absence is the normal shape of the record for a university operating computing plant for its own administrative, teaching and research needs, where nothing is sold and so nothing has to be advertised. The practical consequence for this registry is that the single UNM row should be read as the Information Technologies building on Campus Boulevard, that CARC's Central Avenue facility is a distinct site that is not currently represented, and that the two should not be merged into one entry.
